claims.claim: Machine learning is a subset of artificial intelligence in which programs learn the patterns in training data and make accurate inferences about new data without explicit, hard-coded instructions.
Every machine-learning setup involves three ingredients: data to learn from, a task to get better at, and a way to measure improvement (such as counting errors).

Machine learning differs from conventional programming: a rules-based system needs people to write accurate criteria in advance, while a machine-learning system discovers the patterns itself from a dataset of examples.

Spam filtering illustrates the distinction: a rules-based filter requires manually devised detection criteria, whereas a machine-learned filter is trained on sample emails and learns to identify spam from the examples.
Supervised learning uses labeled training data in which the output is known, while unsupervised learning uses unlabeled data and finds patterns, such as groups, on its own.
Training is the fitting process in which the algorithm adjusts the model to the data (measuring errors as it goes), and using the trained model means applying the fitted pattern to new data.

Machine learning is used in recommendations and personalization, transcription and translation, healthcare diagnostics (including computer vision on medical images and predicting disease from patient records), and fraud detection.
A model's quality is bounded by its training data: poor, noisy, or unrepresentative data leads to poor or untrustworthy outputs, so machine learning is only as good as the data it is fed.
The term machine learning is often attributed to Arthur Samuel's 1959 paper describing a checkers program that learned to play better than the person who wrote it.
Free online courses such as the University of Helsinki's Elements of AI teach the basics of artificial intelligence and machine learning to non-experts without complicated math or programming.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What 'learning' means and how broadly the term is applied.
positions: Google Cloud and IBM define machine learning operationally: performance improves on a task through experience with data, without explicit programming.
The same vendors note that 'machine learning' and 'artificial intelligence' are frequently used interchangeably in popular writing, and that rule-based systems are also called AI.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines learning operationally (measurable improvement on a task through examples) and explicitly warns that the words AI and machine learning are often conflated in marketing, while keeping rule-based AI out of the definition of machine learning.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many families of machine learning to name.
positions: Google Cloud presents four kinds of models: supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning.
IBM organizes the field into supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names only the two big families, supervised and unsupervised, notes that other families exist, and defers all mechanics to the sibling topics supervised-learning and unsupervised-learning.

sourceRecords.title: What is Machine Learning? Types and uses
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. Supports: machine learning as systems that learn and improve without being explicitly programmed; training as optimizing the model to predict the expected outcome with a loss function measuring errors; the fitting process; supervised learning (labeled training data, output known) and unsupervised learning (unlabeled data, groups found by attributes); applications including fraud detection, personalization and recommendations, and transcription and translation; and the warning that machine learning is often only as good as the data it is fed. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
